title: Permutations
tagline: Place each unused element in turn — generate all n! orderings.

intuition.analogy: Seating n guests in a row: choose anyone for seat 1, then anyone remaining for seat 2, and so on. The number of ways is n × (n−1) × … × 1 = n!.
paragraphs: A permutation is an ordering of all elements. Backtracking builds one position at a time: for the current slot, try every element not yet used, recurse, then mark it unused again (backtrack).
A 'used' boolean array (or in-place swapping) prevents reusing an element. When the current arrangement has length n, it's a complete permutation to record.
Unlike subsets (binary choices), permutations branch n-ways at the top, (n−1)-ways next, etc., yielding the factorial explosion — so they're only practical for small n.
intuition.keyIdea: Fill positions left to right, trying each unused element; backtrack by freeing the element after recursing.

steps.title: Track usage
steps.detail: Maintain a used[] flag (or swap elements into place) so each element appears once per permutation.

steps.title: Choose and recurse
steps.detail: For each unused element, mark it used, append to current, recurse; then unmark and pop (backtrack).

steps.title: Record full-length arrangements
steps.detail: When current has n elements, store a copy.

pitfalls: Skipping the 'unmark used' step leaks state across branches.
For duplicates, sort and skip equal unused siblings to avoid repeats.

dryRun.clickMoment: The branching factor shrinks each level: 3 choices, then 2, then 1 — exactly the n! count. Backtracking systematically reuses freed elements down each new branch.

approach: Build permutations by choosing an unused element for each position. A boolean 'used' array tracks availability.
Append to the current path, recurse, then undo. There are n! complete arrangements.

problems.title: Permutations II
problems.hint: Sort; skip a duplicate if its identical predecessor is unused.

approach: Sort so duplicates are adjacent. At each position, skip a value equal to its predecessor when that predecessor hasn't been used in this branch — that prevents generating the same permutation twice.
Otherwise it is the standard used-array backtracking.

problems.title: Next Permutation
problems.statement: Rearrange to the next lexicographic permutation in place.
problems.hint: Find the pivot, swap with the next larger suffix element, reverse the suffix.

approach: Find the rightmost ascent a[i] < a[i+1]. Swap a[i] with the smallest element to its right that is still larger, then reverse the suffix to make it the smallest arrangement.
If no ascent exists, the array is the last permutation; reverse the whole thing.

problems.title: Beautiful Arrangement
problems.statement: Count permutations meeting a divisibility rule.
problems.hint: Backtrack placing positions, pruning invalid choices.

approach: Place numbers 1..n into positions 1..n where position p must hold a value divisible by p or vice-versa.
Backtrack position by position trying each unused number that satisfies the divisibility rule, counting completed arrangements.

problems.title: Letter Tile Possibilities
problems.statement: Count distinct non-empty sequences from tiles.
problems.hint: Backtrack over counts of each letter.

approach: Count distinct non-empty sequences from the tiles. Use a frequency map; at each step pick any letter with remaining count, append it (counts as a sequence), and recurse with one fewer.
The frequency map automatically dedupes identical letters, so we never double-count.
